name: property
intent: Give an object a dynamic, discoverable set of named properties - an indicator-to-value property list with optional descriptors - so instances can gain, lose and expose state at runtime without new classes, at the price of compile-time checking.
problem: An object's attribute set is not fixed when its class is written: it varies per instance or per type (configurable products, user-defined fields, documents that arrive as data), so either every combination needs its own subclass or the class carries the union of all fields and most instances pay for state they never use. Callers must also address those attributes by name at runtime, and tools must be able to discover them.
context: Domain objects whose attributes come from configuration, a database, imported documents or the users themselves rather than from the class designer - configurable products and account types, clinical or research records, document/NoSQL models, plugin annotations - plus the generic tooling (serialization, data binding, reporting) that must enumerate them. It applies where the team accepts runtime checking of names and types in exchange for runtime extensibility, and it is cheapest in languages that already provide runtime-named member access for the pattern to ride on.
benefits: Per-instance state extension: each instance behaves like a lightweight dynamic subclass - properties can be added, changed and removed at runtime without touching the class, and instances that do not carry a property pay nothing for it.

No subclass explosion: one owner class replaces the combinatorial set of simple subtypes that would otherwise differ only in which fields they have (the paper's account case with its ~500 account types).
Runtime configurability: the legal attribute set can come from a schema, configuration, database or end user, which is what makes metadata-driven and adaptive object-model systems possible.

Uniform, discoverable access: one get/set/has/remove/enumerate API plus descriptors lets generic clients - serializers, GUI binders, report writers - treat state the same way without knowing the domain.

Identity-preserving extension: attributes attach to the existing object, so unlike wrapping or decorating the object keeps its identity and its class contract, and the same attribute name can be shared across unrelated classes (black-box extensibility).
Sparse data fits naturally: optional and rarely present attributes are represented by absence instead of by nullable fields carried on every instance.
tradeoffs: Stringly-typed names defeat compile-time checking and refactoring: a typo is a different property (or a runtime failure), the compiler cannot point at the write site, and renaming a key silently breaks distant readers that the IDE cannot find.

Absence must be handled everywhere: clients cannot assume a property exists, and unless the container distinguishes an absent key from a null value, readers cannot tell 'not set' from 'set to nothing', so defaults and validation are re-implemented at each call site.

The interface gets weaker, not just wider: a stored property can no longer be replaced by a computed one without special-casing inside the generic accessor, so encapsulation loses its substitutability guarantee.

Validity is re-invented at runtime: types, ranges, mandatory/optional flags and per-type allowed sets need descriptors or a knowledge level, and each access pays for that checking lookup unless keys become typed objects or array indices.
Per-access and per-instance overhead: every get/set is a hash lookup (often with a copy) rather than a field read, and each instance carries a container even when few instances ever use a property.

Tooling and debugging go blind: state that is not in the class is invisible to static analysis, IDEs and reviewers until a schema or descriptors exist, so typos, missing keys and wrong value types surface late - in production rather than at compile time.
Security surface: keys taken from untrusted input enable mass assignment and, in prototype-based or symbol-keyed runtimes, prototype pollution and unbounded key tables.

participants.responsibility: The object that possesses the properties; owns the property list (usually one per instance, sometimes an external map keyed by instance) and exposes the named access API to clients.
One named attribute: the indicator/value pair stored for a property, created when the property is first set and removed when it is deleted.
The name a property is looked up by - a string or symbol in the flexible form, an immutable typed key object (or PropertyType) in the checked form - and the identity that clients and tools agree on.
The dictionary, hashtable or entry list (alternatively an external instance-to-properties map) that holds the entries and answers get/put/has/remove in average constant time.

Describes what a property means and which values are legal - name, type, default, constraints, display name, accessor references; shared per type as PropertyType/DynaClass/schema and used for validation and discovery.
Code that reads, writes and deletes properties by name; it may be unaware of the mechanism, but it must cope with absent properties and cannot rely on a compile-time contract.

use_cases: Configurable product and account models: insurance, banking or subscription products whose attribute sets differ per variant, instead of one subclass per combination.

Documents that arrive as data: JSON/NoSQL payloads (Kotlin by-map properties, Go map[string]any, Rust serde(flatten), Swift dynamic member lookup over JSON) exposed by name without a hand-written DTO per shape.
User-defined fields in business applications: CRM/ERP extensions where customers add attributes to existing entities without a schema migration.

Metadata-driven GUIs and reports: objects that carry descriptors so a generic binder can render, validate and persist whatever properties the model defines (WPF binding via INotifyPropertyChanged, JavaBeans introspection, schema-driven forms).

Plugin and cross-team annotations: attaching named data to objects owned by another subsystem (GLib keyed data lists, routing slips, timestamp annotations, experiment tags) without changing their classes.
Simulation and game entities whose stats or traits are composed from configuration and change during a run (the burger and character examples of the modern catalog entry).
Sparse domain records: research, clinical or sensor data where only a few attributes are present per instance.
Qt QObject dynamic properties: QObject::setProperty/property and dynamicPropertyNames provide per-instance named state and discovery, while Q_PROPERTY remains the checked contract for stable fields.

GLib/GObject per-instance associations: g_object_set_data()/g_object_get_data() attach string-keyed auxiliary values without changing a type, a useful extension point when bounded keys and explicit lifetime rules are acceptable.

JavaScript reflective objects: Reflect.set()/Reflect.get()/Reflect.ownKeys()/Reflect.getOwnPropertyDescriptor() support runtime named access, enumeration and descriptors, so a schema or allow-list can bound an otherwise open object.
avoid_when: The attribute set is known and stable: declare fields or typed properties - a property list only pays for itself where the set genuinely varies, and a property most instances carry should become a field.
Only a few objects need extra data: keep an external map keyed by identity (Fowler's Extrinsic Property) or a separate typed collection instead of taxing every instance.
The need is behaviour rather than state: attach features with extension-object or decorator, and model per-type attributes explicitly with type-object.

Compile-time guarantees dominate: values with invariants, protocol messages and anything that must be handled exhaustively belong in closed types (algebraic data types, sealed hierarchies) rather than in a name lookup.
The payload is a versioned contract between services: use explicit DTO/message schemas so producers and consumers agree, instead of shipping an open bag of keys.
anti_patterns: Everything-model: all state lives in one property bag and domain logic degenerates into string-key lookups, so behaviour that belonged in the domain is re-implemented (and re-validated) by every caller.

Unvalidated key entry: copying untrusted input keys straight into the property list (mass assignment) or merging arbitrary keys into a prototype-carrying object (prototype pollution), turning configurability into an attack surface.
Magic strings without a schema: property names used as an undocumented, unversioned protocol, so typos, renames and missing defaults fail silently at runtime.
Dynamic properties instead of a schema: using the bag to avoid designing tables or contracts, which pushes joins, validation and reporting rules into every consumer.
Invisible state: no descriptors, no enumeration and no serialization hook, so the object looks empty to tools, reviewers and the next developer.
design_principles: Encapsulation: the owner keeps the storage private and exposes one named-access interface; clients never see the container.
Open/closed: new attributes arrive as data, without modifying the class or adding subtypes.
Information hiding and data-driven design: complexity migrates from code into data (schema and descriptors) that can be inspected and changed at runtime.
Single responsibility: the owner holds state, descriptors hold validity and meaning, clients hold policy.
Explicit interfaces as the counterweight: where the attribute set is stable, prefer intention-revealing properties - the pattern deliberately trades interface strength for flexibility.
best_practices: Keep mandatory, universally present attributes as real fields and put only the open remainder in the property list; promote a property to a field once most instances carry it (the 'finishing school for fields' rule).
Define the key space and its types explicitly - a schema or descriptors, enum-keyed or typed key objects instead of raw strings - and validate on write rather than on every read.
Make absence explicit: use a has/contains check (or an extended lookup) instead of overloading null, and give every property a documented default or error contract.
Expose discovery: enumerate keys, descriptors or dynamic member names so serializers, binders and debugging tools can see the dynamic state.
For untrusted input, filter to an allow-list of keys and never merge raw payload keys into a prototype-carrying object or an unbounded key table.
Isolate the bag at the boundary: convert dynamic documents into typed structures once the shape is known, and keep property bags out of core domain logic.
Treat the key space as versioned: deleting a key leaves stale properties on existing instances, so deprecate rather than remove and document the schema.
